subject: Radiology
q: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to MRI?
why: Claustrophobia is a relative, manageable issue, not an absolute contraindication.
Correct - an incompatible pacemaker can malfunction, heat up, or be dislodged in the MRI field.
Titanium is non-ferromagnetic and MRI-safe.
Pregnancy is not an absolute contraindication to MRI (without gadolinium).
exp: Absolute MRI contraindications include non-MRI-conditional cardiac devices (pacemakers/ICDs), ferromagnetic intracranial aneurysm clips, and cochlear implants not rated MRI-safe - the magnetic field can cause device malfunction, heating, or dislodgement.

subject: Radiology
q: Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus on CT (Holman-Miller sign) is characteristic of which head and neck tumour?
why: Antrochoanal polyp shows a soft-tissue mass through the ostium, not posterior wall bowing.
Esthesioneuroblastoma is an olfactory groove tumour with intracranial extension, a different picture.
Correct - the vascular tumour bows the posterior maxillary wall in adolescent males with epistaxis.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma shows a nasopharyngeal mass with skull-base erosion, not this sign.
exp: Holman-Miller (antral) sign - anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary sinus wall on CT - is a hallmark of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, a locally aggressive vascular tumour of adolescent males presenting with recurrent unilateral epistaxis; biopsy is avoided due to bleeding risk.

subject: Radiology
q: The drooping lily sign on excretory urography (IVU) is seen in which condition?
opts: Duplex renal collecting system with obstructed upper pole moiety
why: A simple renal cyst shows a smooth filling defect, not a displaced collecting system.
Horseshoe kidney shows medially placed lower poles (flower-vase sign), a different finding.
Ureterocele produces a cobra-head sign at the ureteric orifice, not this sign.
Correct - an obstructed, non-functioning upper-pole moiety displaces the lower-pole collecting system downward and laterally.
exp: In duplex kidney with an obstructed/ectopic upper-pole moiety, IVU shows the non-opacified upper moiety displacing the opacified lower-pole calyces downward and laterally - the drooping lily sign.

subject: Radiology
q: The half-life of Cobalt-60, commonly used as a teletherapy source, is approximately:
why: Correct - Cobalt-60 has a physical half-life of about 5.26 years, needing periodic recalibration.
30 years approximates Caesium-137, not Cobalt-60.
8 days is the half-life of Iodine-131.
74 days approximates Iridium-192, used in brachytherapy.
exp: Cobalt-60 teletherapy units require dose-rate recalibration over time because the source decays with a ~5.26-year half-life, unlike linear accelerators which produce X-rays electronically with no radioactive decay to account for.

subject: Radiology
q: A higher-frequency ultrasound transducer (7.5-10 MHz) is preferred for imaging superficial structures such as the thyroid or testis because it provides:
opts: Better resolution but less tissue penetration
Equal resolution and penetration compared to low-frequency probes
No image formation in superficial structures
why: This describes low-frequency probes used for deep structures, the opposite trade-off.
Correct - higher frequency shortens wavelength, improving resolution at the cost of penetration.
Frequency trades resolution against penetration; they are not equal.
High-frequency probes image superficial structures very well; that is their main use.
exp: Ultrasound frequency and penetration are inversely related - higher frequency (7.5-15 MHz) gives excellent resolution for superficial structures (thyroid, testis, neonatal hip) but limited depth, while lower frequency (2-5 MHz) penetrates deeper for abdominal/pelvic imaging at the cost of resolution.

subject: Radiology
q: The investigation of choice to confirm and quantify functional obstruction in suspected ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction is:
why: Shows anatomy and stones, not functional obstruction
Shows collecting system anatomy, not renal function
Correct - assesses differential function and drainage curves
Assesses vesicoureteric reflux, not UPJ obstruction
exp: A diuretic MAG3 renogram assesses differential renal function and drainage curves, distinguishing true functional obstruction from a dilated-but-unobstructed system before deciding on pyeloplasty.

subject: Radiology
q: A snowman or figure-of-8 sign on a neonatal chest X-ray is characteristic of which congenital cardiac anomaly?
opts: Supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous connection (TAPVC)
why: Gives a boot-shaped heart, not a snowman sign
Gives the 3 sign/rib notching, not a snowman sign
Does not classically produce this sign
Correct - classic supracardiac TAPVC finding from the dilated vertical vein and SVC
exp: In supracardiac TAPVC, the dilated vertical vein, left innominate vein, and SVC create a widened superior mediastinal contour resembling a snowman or figure-of-8, typically seen after the first few weeks of life.

subject: Radiology
q: In a patient with suspected gastrointestinal perforation, which contrast agent should be used for imaging instead of barium, to avoid chemical peritonitis?
why: Correct - safe even if it extravasates into the peritoneum
Barium extravasation causes chemical peritonitis and granuloma formation, avoided even diluted
Inadequate for detecting a leak or the perforation site
Gadolinium is an MRI agent, not used for GI luminal contrast studies
exp: Barium is contraindicated when perforation is suspected because free intraperitoneal barium causes severe chemical peritonitis; water-soluble iodinated contrast is used instead as it is safely absorbed if it leaks.

subject: Radiology
q: Which unit measures the equivalent (effective) radiation dose, accounting for the relative biological effectiveness of different radiation types, distinct from the Gray which measures absorbed dose?
why: Measures radioactivity (decay rate), not dose
Correct - the equivalent/effective dose unit used in radiation protection
An older unit of radioactivity, replaced by the Becquerel
Measures exposure (ionization in air), an older unit
exp: The Sievert (Sv) weights absorbed dose in Gray by a radiation-type quality factor and tissue weighting factor to express biological risk or effective dose, and is the unit used for radiation protection limits.

subject: Radiology
q: Which type of renal calculus is radiolucent on a plain X-ray KUB but visible on ultrasound and non-contrast CT?
why: Struvite stones are radiopaque and classically form staghorn calculi
Calcium-containing stones are radiopaque
Correct - classic radiolucent-on-X-ray stone, still detectable on USG/CT
Cystine stones are faintly radiopaque, not classically radiolucent
exp: Uric acid stones lack calcium and are radiolucent on plain X-ray, but remain echogenic on ultrasound and hyperdense on non-contrast CT relative to soft tissue - so CT or USG, not X-ray, is used when they are suspected.

subject: Radiology
q: The imaging principle by which an ultrasound transducer converts electrical energy into mechanical sound waves and back is called the:
why: Correct: piezoelectric crystals in the transducer convert electrical energy to mechanical vibrations and back for image formation
Compton effect describes photon scattering with energy loss, relevant to X-ray and tissue interaction, not ultrasound generation
Photoelectric effect describes complete photon absorption ejecting an electron, relevant to X-ray and CT contrast, not ultrasound generation
Doppler effect describes the frequency shift used to measure blood flow velocity, not the transducer's basic sound-generation mechanism
exp: Ultrasound transducers contain piezoelectric crystals that convert electrical energy to mechanical sound vibrations to generate the beam, and convert returning echo vibrations back to electrical signals for image formation, the fundamental principle of ultrasound imaging.

subject: Radiology
q: A congenital neck swelling located along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle in a young adult, confirmed as cystic on imaging, is most likely a:
why: Cystic hygroma is typically a large multiloculated posterior triangle mass presenting in infancy, not along the SCM border in a young adult
Correct: second branchial cleft cysts classically present along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid in young adults
Thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline swelling that moves with tongue protrusion or swallowing, not lateral along SCM
Ranula is a floor-of-mouth or sublingual cystic swelling, not a lateral neck mass
exp: Second branchial cleft cysts, the commonest branchial anomaly, classically present as a painless cystic neck mass along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid in young adults, often noticed after an upper respiratory infection, and appear as a well-defined cystic lesion on CT, MRI, or ultrasound.

subject: Radiology
q: On contrast-enhanced CT of an incidentally detected adrenal mass, an absolute contrast washout of more than 60% at 10-15 minutes is characteristic of a:
why: Adrenal metastases typically show slower washout, less than 60% absolute, overlapping with other malignant lesions
Pheochromocytoma is typically hypervascular with heterogeneous enhancement and slow washout, not rapid washout
Correct: benign adrenal adenomas are lipid-rich and show rapid contrast washout exceeding 60% absolute
Adrenocortical carcinoma is typically large and heterogeneous with slow or incomplete washout
exp: Benign adrenal adenomas are lipid-rich and show rapid contrast washout on delayed CT, with absolute washout exceeding 60% and relative washout exceeding 40%, distinguishing them from malignant or metastatic adrenal lesions which tend to retain contrast, a key non-invasive CT criterion for characterizing adrenal incidentalomas.

subject: Radiology
q: Cells are most radiosensitive during which phase of the cell cycle, a principle exploited in fractionated radiotherapy?
why: G0 quiescent cells are relatively radioresistant, one reason slow-growing tumours and normal tissues respond differently to radiation
S phase, especially late S, is the most radioresistant phase due to active DNA repair capacity
G1 phase is intermediate in radiosensitivity, less sensitive than G2/M
Correct: G2/M phase, mitosis, is the most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle
exp: Cells are most radiosensitive in the G2/M phase, mitosis, and late G1, and most radioresistant in late S phase; fractionated radiotherapy exploits redistribution of surviving cells into more radiosensitive phases between fractions, one of the classic 4 Rs of radiobiology.

subject: Radiology
q: Adjusting the CT window width and window level to selectively display lung parenchyma detail versus soft tissue detail on the same scan is called:
why: Correct: windowing selects a Hounsfield unit range and center to optimize grayscale contrast for a specific tissue
Multiplanar reconstruction creates coronal or sagittal images from axial data, a different post-processing step unrelated to grayscale display range
Beam hardening correction addresses an artifact from preferential absorption of lower-energy photons, not display windowing
Reformatting is a general term for reconstructing images in different planes, not the specific HU display range concept
exp: CT windowing selects a range of Hounsfield units, the window width, centered on a chosen value, the window level, to optimize grayscale contrast for a specific tissue, such as a wide low-level lung window versus a narrow higher-level soft-tissue window, without re-scanning the patient.

subject: Radiology
q: A 55-year-old woman with recent hip surgery develops sudden dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain. Chest X-ray shows a focal area of oligaemia (relative lucency) distal to an abrupt vascular cut-off. This finding is known as:
why: Hampton hump is a peripheral pleural-based wedge opacity from pulmonary infarction, a later finding, not this
Correct - abrupt vessel cut-off with distal lucency defines Westermark sign
Fleischner sign is focal enlargement of the occluded pulmonary artery, the opposite pattern (increased, not decreased, vessel prominence)
Palla sign is enlargement of the right descending pulmonary artery, again a prominence sign, not an oligaemia sign
exp: Westermark sign is focal oligaemia distal to an occluded pulmonary artery in acute PE - a plain-film clue that is subtle and easily missed, so a normal CXR never rules out PE.

subject: Radiology
q: Gadolinium-based MRI contrast agents should be avoided, or used with extreme caution, in patients with:
opts: eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73m squared (risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis)
Pregnancy in the first trimester only
A known history of iodinated-contrast allergy
why: Correct - NSF risk is the specific, gadolinium-related caution
Gadolinium is avoided throughout pregnancy when possible, not just trimester 1, and this isn't the classic teaching point
Iodinated-contrast allergy does not predict gadolinium reaction - the two agent classes are chemically unrelated
Pacemakers are a general MRI-safety issue (device compatibility), not specific to the contrast agent
exp: Severe renal impairment is the key contraindication to gadolinium because free gadolinium ion deposition in tissue causes nephrogenic systemic fibrosis (NSF), a fibrosing skin/organ disease seen almost exclusively in patients with eGFR under 30 or on dialysis.

subject: Radiology
q: A 4-year-old presents with chronic mouth breathing, snoring, and hyponasal speech. A lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph is most useful to assess:
opts: Adenoid size and nasopharyngeal airway (adenoid-nasopharyngeal ratio)
why: Tonsillar crypts are an oral-cavity clinical finding, not seen on this radiograph
Vocal cord mobility needs laryngoscopy or dynamic imaging, not a static lateral neck film
Correct - the adenoid-nasopharyngeal (A/N) ratio is read directly off this view
Thyroid size is assessed by ultrasound/palpation, not a soft-tissue neck X-ray
exp: A lateral neck soft-tissue film is a simple, low-dose way to estimate adenoid bulk against the nasopharyngeal airway column before deciding on adenoidectomy - tonsils themselves are assessed clinically, not radiographically.

subject: Radiology
q: Hypoxic tumour cells are relatively radioresistant compared with well-oxygenated cells. This phenomenon is quantified by the:
why: RBE compares the biological effect of different radiation types at equal physical dose, unrelated to oxygenation
Therapeutic ratio compares tumour lethal dose to normal-tissue tolerance dose, a different concept
LET describes energy deposited per unit track length, a physical not an oxygenation-dependent property
Correct - OER is precisely this oxygen-dependent radiosensitivity ratio
exp: Oxygen fixes DNA damage caused by radiation-generated free radicals, so hypoxic tumour cores (common in bulky/necrotic tumours) resist radiotherapy - OER (typically about 2.5 to 3 for X-rays) expresses how many times more dose a hypoxic cell needs for the same kill as an oxygenated one.

subject: Radiology
q: HRCT chest in a patient with active pulmonary tuberculosis shows centrilobular nodules with branching linear opacities resembling a budding tree. This pattern is called:
why: Correct - this is the textbook description of tree-in-bud from endobronchial TB spread
Lymphangitic carcinomatosis shows smooth/nodular interlobular septal thickening, not centrilobular budding
Alveolar proteinosis shows crazy-paving (ground-glass with septal thickening), a different pattern
UIP shows peripheral, basal honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis, not tree-in-bud
exp: Tree-in-bud on HRCT reflects mucopurulent material impacting small centrilobular bronchioles - classically endobronchial spread of TB, but also seen in other endobronchial infections (bacterial bronchopneumonia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, cystic fibrosis).

subject: Radiology
q: Ultrasound of a midline neck swelling just below the hyoid bone in a 6-year-old shows a well-defined cystic lesion that moves cranially with tongue protrusion and on swallowing. Diagnosis?
why: Correct — midline location plus movement with tongue protrusion is the defining sign of a thyroglossal duct cyst.
Branchial cleft cyst is lateral (anterior to sternocleidomastoid), not midline, and does not move with tongue protrusion.
Cystic hygroma is a lateral, multiloculated, trans-illuminant lymphatic malformation, usually in the posterior triangle.
Dermoid cyst is also midline but is a firm, non-mobile subcutaneous lesion that does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion.
exp: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a remnant of the thyroid gland's descent along the thyroglossal tract from the foramen cecum to its final pretracheal position; because it stays tethered to the hyoid bone, it is the classic midline paediatric neck swelling that moves upward with tongue protrusion and swallowing — the single sonographic clue that separates it from branchial cleft cysts, cystic hygromas, and dermoid cysts.

subject: Radiology
q: An intravenous urogram shows a smooth, round filling defect at the distal ureteric orifice surrounded by a radiolucent halo, giving a cobra head appearance within the bladder. Diagnosis?
why: PUV shows a dilated posterior urethra on VCUG (spinning top sign), not a bladder filling defect.
VUR shows retrograde contrast into the ureter/pelvis on VCUG, not a cobra-head sign.
Correct — pathognomonic cobra-head/spring-onion appearance of a ureterocele on IVU.
UPJ obstruction shows a dilated renal pelvis with abrupt cutoff at the pelviureteric junction, not a bladder-level sign.
exp: A ureterocele is cystic dilatation of the submucosal distal ureter ballooning into the bladder lumen. Contrast filling the dilated segment, surrounded by a lucent rim of bladder mucosa, produces the classic cobra head (or spring onion) sign on IVU/VCUG — a quick visual diagnosis worth memorising as an image-based one-liner.

subject: Radiology
q: A chest X-ray in an infant shows a curvilinear soft-tissue density running along the right heart border, resembling a Turkish sword, associated with an anomalous pulmonary vein draining into the IVC. Sign?
why: Snowman/figure-of-8 sign is seen in supracardiac TAPVC from the dilated vertical vein and SVC.
Sail sign refers to the neonatal thymic shadow, not a venous anomaly.
Water-bottle sign describes a globular cardiac silhouette in pericardial effusion.
Correct — scimitar sign is the curved shadow of the anomalously draining right pulmonary vein in scimitar syndrome.
exp: The scimitar sign is the curved, sword-like shadow of an anomalous right pulmonary vein coursing toward the IVC, seen in scimitar syndrome — a form of partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection often accompanied by right lung hypoplasia and dextroposition of the heart.

subject: Radiology
q: The Gray (Gy), the SI unit used to express absorbed radiation dose in radiotherapy, is defined as which of the following?
opts: 1 joule of energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue
100 rad absorbed per kilogram of tissue
1 coulomb of charge per kilogram of air
why: Correct — the Gray is defined as 1 joule of energy deposited per kilogram of matter.
Reverses the true relationship — 1 Gy equals 100 rad, not a rate expressed this way.
Coulomb/kg is the unit of exposure (Roentgen-related), not absorbed dose.
Confuses absorbed dose with dose rate; the Gray itself has no time component.
exp: The Gray is the SI unit of absorbed radiation dose, defined as 1 joule of energy deposited per kilogram of matter. It replaced the older CGS unit rad, with the conversion 1 Gy = 100 rad — a fast recall fact for radiotherapy basics.

subject: Radiology
q: A neonate has episodes of cyanosis that worsen during feeding and improve with crying. CT of the nose shows bony narrowing of the posterior nasal aperture bilaterally. Diagnosis?
why: Laryngomalacia causes inspiratory stridor worsening with feeding/supine positioning, not cyclical crying-relieved cyanosis.
Subglottic stenosis causes biphasic stridor, not this crying-relieved cyanosis pattern.
Correct — bilateral choanal atresia in an obligate nasal breather causes cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying and worsened by feeding, confirmed on thin-section CT.
Vascular ring causes stridor/dysphagia from tracheoesophageal compression, not nasal obstruction.
exp: Neonates are obligate nasal breathers, so bilateral choanal atresia produces cyclical cyanosis that is relieved by crying (mouth breathing takes over) and worsened during feeding (nose obstructed while sucking). Thin-section CT is the confirmatory test, showing bony or mixed bony-membranous obstruction of the posterior choana.

subject: Radiology
q: In a hemodynamically unstable trauma patient with suspected pneumothorax, which imaging modality is preferred for rapid bedside diagnosis, avoiding the need to move the patient or expose them to radiation?
why: Correct — fast, safe, and bedside-capable in unstable patients
Expiratory CXR is slower to obtain, requires patient positioning, and is less sensitive than USG for small pneumothoraces
CT requires transport of an unstable patient and carries radiation exposure
V/Q scanning is used for suspected pulmonary embolism, not pneumothorax, and is impractical in acute trauma
exp: Bedside eFAST ultrasound can rapidly detect pneumothorax by identifying loss of lung sliding and the 'lung point' sign, without moving an unstable patient or exposing them to ionizing radiation — faster and safer than CT or plain radiography in this emergency setting.

subject: Radiology
q: In a patient with a suspected metallic intraorbital or intraocular foreign body, which imaging modality should be AVOIDED as the initial investigation?
opts: CT scan, due to radiation exposure
Plain X-ray, due to poor sensitivity
MRI, due to risk of magnetic displacement of the foreign body causing further injury
why: CT's radiation exposure is an acceptable trade-off given it is the safest imaging option here, not a reason to avoid it
Plain X-ray is a reasonable initial screening tool, not one to be avoided, though less precise than CT
Correct — the specific safety contraindication
Ultrasound is not contraindicated, merely less precise for foreign body localization
exp: MRI is contraindicated as the initial investigation when a metallic/ferromagnetic intraorbital or intraocular foreign body is suspected, because the strong magnetic field can cause the foreign body to move, worsening ocular or orbital injury; CT is preferred to localize and characterize it.

subject: Radiology
q: In acute unilateral ureteric obstruction, the affected kidney classically shows which finding on IVU or CT urography?
opts: Delayed and persistently dense nephrogram (the 'obstructive nephrogram')
Wedge-shaped hypodense area on contrast CT
why: Correct — the classic obstructive uropathy sign
An absent nephrogram suggests arterial occlusion/non-perfusion, not obstruction
Cortical rim sign is seen in renal infarction, sparing a thin peripheral rim supplied by capsular collaterals
A wedge-shaped hypodense area is the classic CT appearance of renal infarction, not obstruction
exp: In acute ureteric obstruction, glomerular filtration continues against raised intratubular pressure with slowed transit, producing a nephrogram that appears later than normal but becomes progressively denser and more prolonged — in contrast to renal artery occlusion, which produces an absent or markedly faint nephrogram.

subject: Radiology
q: As per the Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau, which type of cells are most radiosensitive?
opts: Rapidly dividing, undifferentiated cells with a long mitotic future
Cells with low oxygen tension (hypoxic cells)
Cells arrested in the G0 resting phase
why: Slowly dividing, well-differentiated cells (e.g., neurons, muscle) are relatively radioresistant, the opposite of the law's prediction
Correct — the law's defining statement
Hypoxic cells are actually relatively radioresistant (the oxygen effect), an important but separate radiobiological principle
G0 cells are relatively radioresistant since radiosensitivity peaks in actively cycling (G2/M) phases
exp: The Law of Bergonié and Tribondeau states that tissue radiosensitivity is directly proportional to the rate of cell division and inversely proportional to the degree of differentiation — rapidly dividing, undifferentiated tissues are the most radiosensitive, forming the biological rationale for fractionated radiotherapy.

subject: Radiology
q: In a child with suspected acute appendicitis, which imaging modality is preferred as the first-line investigation to avoid ionizing radiation exposure, reserving CT for equivocal cases?
why: Plain X-ray has poor sensitivity/specificity for appendicitis and is not the recommended first-line study
MRI is a reasonable second-line, radiation-free alternative when USG is equivocal, but is not first-line due to cost/availability
CT is highly accurate but carries radiation exposure, so it is reserved for equivocal cases, not used first-line
Correct — the radiation-free first-line study
exp: Graded-compression ultrasonography (looking for a non-compressible tubular structure >6 mm with a target sign) is recommended as the first-line imaging study for suspected paediatric appendicitis, per the ALARA principle, with CT or MRI reserved for equivocal cases.

subject: Radiology
q: Salivary gland calculi (sialolithiasis) most commonly occur in which gland/duct, and what explains this predilection?
opts: Parotid gland/Stensen's duct, because of its serous secretion
Sublingual gland, because of its location
Submandibular gland/Wharton's duct, because its secretion is more mucous/alkaline and calcium-rich, and the duct runs uphill against gravity
why: The parotid's serous, lower-calcium secretion makes it far less prone to stone formation compared to the submandibular gland.
The sublingual gland is a rare site for calculi and not the classic answer for sialolithiasis.
Correct — the submandibular gland/Wharton's duct is by far the most common site of sialolithiasis for the reasons given.
Sialolithiasis is markedly more common in the submandibular gland, not equally distributed across all glands.
exp: Roughly 80-90% of salivary calculi occur in the submandibular gland/Wharton's duct — the secretion is more mucous, alkaline, and calcium/phosphate-rich than the parotid's serous secretion, and Wharton's duct's longer, tortuous, uphill course predisposes to stasis and stone impaction. Non-contrast CT is the imaging investigation of choice, as most stones are radiopaque.

subject: Radiology
q: On abdominal ultrasound of a 3-year-old with an asymptomatic abdominal mass, a large, well-defined intrarenal mass is seen with a rim of compressed, displaced normal renal parenchyma visible at its margin. This "claw sign" is characteristic of which tumor, and what does it help distinguish?
opts: Neuroblastoma; it helps distinguish it from a renal-origin mass
Hepatoblastoma; it helps distinguish it from a splenic mass
Rhabdomyosarcoma; it helps distinguish it from a bladder mass
Wilms tumor; it helps confirm the mass is of renal (not extrarenal) origin
why: Neuroblastoma is an extrarenal (adrenal/sympathetic chain) mass that displaces the kidney without a claw sign, since it doesn't arise from renal parenchyma.
Hepatoblastoma is a hepatic mass and is not associated with the renal claw sign.
Rhabdomyosarcoma of the bladder/genitourinary tract has different imaging features and is not associated with this sign.
Correct — the claw sign confirms renal origin, classically described for Wilms tumor.
exp: The "claw sign" (or "beak sign") is a rim of normal, compressed renal parenchyma wrapping around a large intrarenal mass, confirming the mass arises from within the kidney itself — classically Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma), the commonest renal malignancy of childhood — helping distinguish it from an extrarenal mass like neuroblastoma, which displaces rather than arises from the kidney.

subject: Radiology
q: In a critically ill, supine trauma patient unable to have an erect chest X-ray, an abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic angle on the supine film is a subtle but important sign of which condition?
why: Pleural effusion on a supine film causes a diffuse haziness/increased density over the affected hemithorax, not a deep lucent sulcus.
Consolidation appears as increased opacity with air bronchograms, not increased lucency at the costophrenic angle.
Pulmonary edema shows bilateral perihilar haziness and Kerley B lines, not a deep lucent sulcus.
Correct — the deep sulcus sign on a supine film is a key indicator of pneumothorax.
exp: On a supine chest X-ray, free pleural air rises to the least dependent part of the thorax — anteriorly and inferiorly rather than apically as on an erect film — producing an abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic sulcus ("deep sulcus sign"). Recognizing this is critical in supine trauma imaging, where a missed tension pneumothorax can be rapidly fatal.

subject: Radiology
q: Conventional external beam radiotherapy delivers the total tumoricidal dose in small daily fractions (e.g., 2 Gy/day, 5 days/week) rather than as a single large dose. Which principle of radiobiology does this fractionation schedule primarily exploit to spare normal tissue?
opts: Reoxygenation of hypoxic tumor cells between fractions
Differential repair of sublethal damage — normal cells repair more efficiently than tumor cells between fractions
Redistribution of tumor cells into radiosensitive phases of the cell cycle
Repopulation of normal tissue stem cells between fractions
why: Reoxygenation (previously hypoxic tumor cells becoming better oxygenated between fractions) is one of the 4 Rs, but it primarily improves tumor control rather than sparing normal tissue.
Correct — normal tissue's superior capacity for sublethal damage repair between fractions is the main basis for normal-tissue sparing with fractionation.
Redistribution refers to tumor cells cycling into more radiosensitive phases between fractions, aiding tumor kill, not normal-tissue sparing per se.
Repopulation refers to surviving clonogenic cells proliferating during treatment — protective for normal tissue but not the principal rationale usually cited for the sparing seen with fractionation.
exp: Fractionation is designed around the "4 Rs" of radiobiology (Repair, Reassortment, Repopulation, Reoxygenation). The principle most directly responsible for normal-tissue sparing with small daily fractions is that normal cells repair sublethal radiation damage more efficiently than tumor cells between fractions, widening the therapeutic window over the course of treatment.

subject: Radiology
q: On a lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray of a febrile 3-year-old with neck stiffness and odynophagia, widening of the prevertebral soft tissue space anterior to the cervical vertebrae is most suggestive of which diagnosis?
why: Epiglottitis shows the "thumb sign" — a swollen, rounded epiglottis on lateral neck X-ray — not prevertebral widening.
Adenoid hypertrophy causes nasopharyngeal airway narrowing visible on lateral neck film, not prevertebral soft tissue widening.
Correct — prevertebral soft tissue widening is the classic sign of retropharyngeal abscess.
Croup shows the "steeple sign" of subglottic tracheal narrowing on frontal neck X-ray, not prevertebral widening on the lateral view.
exp: Widening of the prevertebral soft tissue space on a lateral neck X-ray (taken in inspiration with the neck extended, to avoid a false-positive from flexion/expiration) is the key sign of retropharyngeal abscess — a deep neck space infection typically following pharyngitis in young children, presenting with fever, neck stiffness/torticollis, odynophagia, and drooling, requiring prompt contrast CT confirmation and ENT input.

subject: Radiology
q: Which imaging investigation is used to diagnose and grade vesicoureteric reflux (Grade I-V) in children?
why: Ultrasound can suggest hydronephrosis/hydroureter but cannot dynamically grade reflux
DMSA assesses renal cortical scarring/differential function, a consequence of VUR, not a grading tool
CT urography is used for anatomical/functional renal imaging, not standard VUR grading in children due to radiation
Correct - MCUG visualizes retrograde contrast flow during voiding, allowing VUR grading
exp: MCUG involves catheterizing the bladder, instilling contrast, and imaging during voiding to visualize retrograde contrast flow into the ureters/renal pelvis, allowing grading of VUR from Grade I (ureter only) to Grade V (gross dilatation with tortuosity); it also detects posterior urethral valves in boys.

subject: Radiology
q: On ultrasound, hydronephrosis showing dilated calyces with loss of normal papillary impressions and cortical thinning corresponds to which SFU (Society for Fetal Urology) grade?
why: Correct - cortical thinning marks the most severe SFU grade
Grade I is mild, pelvis-only dilation
Grade II adds calyceal dilation without cortical change
Grade III shows all calyces dilated but the cortex is preserved
exp: SFU grading of hydronephrosis: 0 = no dilation, I = pelvis only, II = pelvis plus a few calyces, III = pelvis plus all calyces dilated, IV = grade III features plus cortical thinning - the most severe grade.

subject: Radiology
q: Investigation of choice for a patient presenting with acute flank pain suspected to be due to a ureteric stone?
why: IVU is largely replaced due to contrast exposure and longer acquisition time
Correct — highest sensitivity, detects radiolucent stones too
Plain X-ray misses radiolucent (uric acid) stones and overlying bowel gas obscures small stones
USG avoids radiation and is preferred in pregnancy/children, but has lower sensitivity for ureteric stones than NCCT
exp: Non-contrast CT KUB detects over 95% of stones of any composition, needs no contrast, and is fast — now the standard investigation of choice for acute renal colic in adults.

subject: Radiology
q: The principle of keeping radiation exposure As Low As Reasonably Achievable while still obtaining a diagnostic image is known by which acronym?
why: Not a standard radiology term
Correct
Not a standard radiology term
LNT (linear no-threshold) is a separate radiobiological dose-response model, not the exposure-minimisation principle
exp: ALARA is the core radiation-protection principle guiding imaging practice — using the lowest dose that still yields a diagnostically adequate image, via shielding, collimation, and justified test selection; it underlies why USG/MRI are preferred over CT in children and pregnancy.

subject: Radiology
q: Which imaging modality is preferred for characterizing a parotid gland mass such as a suspected pleomorphic adenoma?
opts: MRI, for its superior soft-tissue contrast and delineation of facial nerve/deep-lobe extension
Ultrasonography, as the first-line screening modality for a palpable parotid mass
CT scan, better suited to assessing bony erosion than soft-tissue extent
Sialography, mainly useful for evaluating salivary duct obstruction rather than a mass
why: Correct
USG is a reasonable first-line screen for a palpable mass but cannot assess deep-lobe extension or the facial nerve relationship
CT shows bony erosion well but has inferior soft-tissue contrast compared to MRI
Sialography assesses ductal pathology (sialolithiasis, sialadenitis), not mass characterisation
exp: MRI is the imaging investigation of choice for characterising a parotid gland mass because of its superior soft-tissue contrast, allowing accurate delineation of tumor extent, differentiation of superficial from deep lobe involvement, and assessment of the mass's relationship to the facial nerve and parapharyngeal space — critical for planning superficial versus total parotidectomy.

subject: Radiology
q: Chest X-ray showing numerous small, uniformly distributed 1-3 mm nodules ('millet seed' pattern) diffusely throughout both lung fields is characteristic of which condition?
why: Pneumoconiosis shows upper-zone nodules, possibly with eggshell calcification, a different distribution
Correct — miliary TB shows diffuse uniform millet-seed nodules from hematogenous spread
Bronchiectasis shows dilated, thickened bronchi ('tram-track'/'signet ring'), not diffuse tiny nodules
Sarcoidosis classically shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with reticulonodular change, not uniform miliary spread
exp: Miliary tuberculosis results from hematogenous dissemination of M. tuberculosis, producing innumerable tiny (1-3 mm), uniformly distributed nodules resembling millet seeds throughout both lung fields — it indicates disseminated disease and warrants prompt anti-tubercular therapy plus evaluation for extrapulmonary (especially CNS/meningeal) involvement.

subject: Radiology
q: On which MRI sequence does fat appear bright while cerebrospinal fluid appears dark, giving good anatomical detail?
why: T2-weighted images show fluid (including CSF) as bright, the opposite pattern
FLAIR is T2-based with CSF signal suppressed, used to highlight periventricular lesions, not defined by bright fat
Correct — T1-weighted shows bright fat, dark CSF, good anatomical detail
DWI highlights restricted water diffusion (e.g., acute infarct), unrelated to this pattern
exp: On T1-weighted MRI, fat is bright and water/CSF is dark, giving good anatomical/structural detail; on T2-weighted images the pattern reverses (fluid bright), better for detecting edema/pathology — 'T1 = anatomy, T2 = pathology (fluid bright)' is a common mnemonic.

subject: Radiology
q: Best initial imaging modality to evaluate a suspected orbital floor blow-out fracture with muscle entrapment is:
opts: Thin-section CT orbit with coronal reconstructions
why: Plain X-ray is poorly sensitive for floor fractures/entrapment
USG has no role in bony orbital trauma
Correct - best shows fracture line and entrapment
MRI is not first-line for acute bony trauma
exp: Thin-section CT of the orbit with coronal reconstructions is the imaging of choice for blow-out fractures, showing the fracture line and herniated orbital fat/muscle with entrapment.

subject: Radiology
q: Investigation of choice to assess ossicular erosion and complications in a case of suspected cholesteatoma prior to surgery is:
why: Plain X-ray mastoid views are outdated and insensitive for bony detail
MRI is mainly used to detect recurrent/residual disease postoperatively, not the primary preoperative bony study
USG has no role in temporal bone bony anatomy
Correct - HRCT provides the detailed bony anatomy needed for surgical planning
exp: HRCT temporal bone is the standard preoperative imaging for cholesteatoma, delineating ossicular chain erosion, facial nerve canal dehiscence, tegmen tympani erosion, and semicircular canal fistula - essential surgical planning information; MRI (non-EPI diffusion-weighted sequences) is complementary, mainly used to detect recurrent or residual disease postoperatively.

subject: Radiology
q: In acute scrotal pain, color Doppler ultrasound showing absent or markedly reduced blood flow to the testis is characteristic of: Image described: testicular parenchyma with no detectable intratesticular color flow signal on Doppler.
why: Epididymo-orchitis shows increased flow (hyperemia), the opposite finding
Hydrocele is a fluid collection, not a vascular flow abnormality
Varicocele shows dilated venous flow in the pampiniform plexus, not absent arterial flow
Correct - torsion cuts off arterial supply, producing this Doppler finding
exp: Color Doppler ultrasound is the key emergency investigation distinguishing testicular torsion (absent/reduced flow, a surgical emergency) from epididymo-orchitis (increased flow, treated medically) in acute scrotal pain; time is critical, as testicular salvage rates fall sharply after about 6 hours of ischemia.

subject: Radiology
q: On CT imaging, water is assigned a Hounsfield unit (HU) value of 0 by convention. Which of the following best represents the approximate HU value of dense cortical bone?
why: -1000 HU corresponds to air, not bone
-100 HU corresponds approximately to fat, not bone
+40 HU is typical for soft tissue/muscle, not dense bone
Correct — dense bone shows the highest, strongly positive HU values
exp: The Hounsfield scale calibrates air at approximately -1000 HU and water at 0 HU; fat lies slightly negative (around -100 HU), most soft tissues cluster around +20 to +80 HU, and dense cortical bone shows the highest attenuation, approximately +1000 HU or more — this underlies CT windowing choices for image interpretation.

subject: Radiology
q: Which nuclear imaging study is considered the gold standard for detecting renal cortical scarring following an episode of acute pyelonephritis or in children with vesicoureteral reflux?
why: DTPA assesses GFR and drainage/obstruction (dynamic renogram), not cortical scarring
MAG3 is also a dynamic tracer for drainage/obstruction, not scarring
Correct, DMSA is a static cortical tracer, the gold standard for detecting and quantifying renal scarring
IVU can show scarring indirectly but is far less sensitive than DMSA
exp: DMSA scanning is used both in the acute phase (to detect acute pyelonephritis as photopenic areas) and at 4-6 months post-infection (to assess permanent scarring), guiding decisions about further reflux workup and long-term follow-up in children with recurrent UTI/VUR.

subject: Radiology
q: Image described: CT urogram delayed-phase image showing contrast opacifying the renal pelvis, ureters, and bladder. This excretory phase, acquired 5-15 minutes after contrast injection, is essential for optimal visualization of which structures?
opts: Renal collecting system, ureters, and bladder
why: Correct — the delayed/excretory phase shows contrast-opacified collecting system, ureters, and bladder, ideal for urothelial pathology.
Wrong — cortical enhancement pattern is best seen on the earlier corticomedullary phase.
Wrong — renal artery anatomy is best seen on the arterial/corticomedullary phase, not the delayed excretory phase.
Wrong — adrenal characterization uses a dedicated adrenal washout protocol, not the excretory urographic phase.
exp: CT urography phases: unenhanced (detects calculi), corticomedullary (roughly 25-70 seconds, parenchymal/vascular detail), nephrographic (roughly 100 seconds, best for mass detection), and excretory/delayed (5-15 minutes, contrast excreted into the collecting system/ureters/bladder) — this last phase is essential for evaluating urothelial lesions, filling defects, and collecting-system anatomy.

subject: Radiology
q: Which of the following imaging modalities does NOT use ionizing radiation?
why: CT uses rotating X-ray tubes, a major ionizing-radiation source
Fluoroscopy is continuous real-time X-ray, high cumulative dose
correct — MRI has zero ionizing radiation
Mammography is a low-dose but still X-ray-based technique
exp: MRI uses a magnetic field and radiofrequency pulses to image hydrogen nuclei — no ionizing radiation at all, which is why it is preferred in pregnancy (after the first trimester, with caution) and for repeated paediatric follow-up imaging. CT, fluoroscopy, and mammography all use X-rays.

subject: Radiology
q: Kerley B lines on a chest radiograph — short, horizontal, peripheral lines at the costophrenic angles — indicate which underlying pathology?
why: Lobar pneumonia shows consolidation with air bronchograms, not septal lines.
Correct — Kerley B lines are a sign of interstitial pulmonary edema.
Pneumothorax shows an absent peripheral lung marking with a visible visceral pleural edge.
Pulmonary embolism classically shows Westermark sign or Hampton's hump, not Kerley B lines.
exp: Kerley B lines represent thickened interlobular septa from fluid, a sign of raised pulmonary venous pressure and interstitial edema — classically seen in left heart failure or mitral stenosis.

subject: Radiology
q: On contrast-enhanced CT, a renal cyst shows thickened irregular septa with measurable enhancement but no solid enhancing nodular component. As per the Bosniak classification, how should this lesion be managed?
opts: Reassure and no follow-up needed (Bosniak I)
Surgical excision given significant malignancy risk (Bosniak III)
Immediate radical nephrectomy without further workup
why: Bosniak I is a simple anechoic cyst with a hairline-thin wall and no septa - doesn't match this description
Bosniak IIF has minimally thickened septa without measurable enhancement and only needs surveillance, whereas this lesion shows measurable enhancement
Correct - thick irregular enhancing septa without a solid nodule places this in Bosniak III, with roughly 50 percent malignancy risk warranting excision
Even Bosniak III/IV lesions are generally managed with partial nephrectomy or further characterization, not blind radical nephrectomy without workup
exp: The Bosniak classification stratifies renal cystic lesions by CT features to predict malignancy: category I and II are benign with no follow-up; IIF (minimal septal thickening, no measurable enhancement) needs surveillance; III (thick irregular enhancing septa/walls, roughly 50% malignant) warrants surgical excision; IV (solid enhancing components) is treated as cancer. Measurable septal enhancement with irregular thickening upgrades a lesion to category III.

subject: Radiology
q: A boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) appearance on chest X-ray is classically seen in which congenital cardiac lesion?
why: Correct - RVH with an upturned apex plus a concave pulmonary artery segment from pulmonary stenosis gives the boot-shaped heart of Tetralogy of Fallot.
Transposition of the great arteries shows an egg-on-side appearance from a narrow superior mediastinum.
Supracardiac TAPVC shows the snowman or figure-of-8 sign.
Pericardial effusion produces a globular water bottle cardiac silhouette.
exp: Boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot) - upturned cardiac apex from RVH plus a concave pulmonary artery segment from pulmonary stenosis/infundibular narrowing - is the classic chest X-ray sign of Tetralogy of Fallot. Contrast with egg-on-side (TGA), snowman sign (TAPVC), and water bottle sign (pericardial effusion) as paired radiology one-liners.

subject: Radiology
q: Image described: Lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray in a toxic-looking 4-year-old child showing a swollen, rounded epiglottis. What is this radiographic sign called?
exp: The thumb sign on a lateral neck X-ray represents a swollen epiglottis and is classic for acute epiglottitis, an airway emergency where oral or throat examination should be avoided until the airway is secured. Do not confuse with the steeple sign of subglottic narrowing seen in croup.

subject: Radiology
q: On ultrasound, which longitudinal-section sign of intussusception is the counterpart of the transverse 'target/doughnut' sign, formed by alternating hyper- and hypoechoic layers of bowel wall?
why: Correct: the pseudokidney/sandwich sign is the longitudinal view of the same layered, telescoped bowel.
Wrong: rat tail sign is a tapering contrast column (e.g. achalasia), not an intussusception ultrasound sign.
Wrong: string sign is a narrowed contrast column (pyloric stenosis, Crohn disease).
Wrong: comet tail is a reverberation artefact (e.g. gallbladder adenomyomatosis).
exp: The pseudokidney or sandwich sign is the longitudinal-section counterpart of the transverse target/doughnut sign - both are produced by the same telescoped, layered bowel wall, just viewed from different planes. Recognising both views matters because a probe angle that only catches one plane can otherwise miss the diagnosis.

subject: Radiology
q: The "spinning top" appearance of the posterior urethra on a micturating cystourethrogram is classically seen in which condition?
exp: In posterior urethral valves — a congenital obstructing membrane seen only in male infants — the voiding cystourethrogram shows an elongated, dilated posterior urethra tapering abruptly at the valve, giving the classic 'spinning top' or 'keyhole' appearance, usually with a thickened, trabeculated bladder wall. Early recognition matters because ongoing obstruction can cause irreversible renal damage.

subject: Radiology
q: Which chest X-ray sign describes bilateral hilar and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy, classically seen in stage I sarcoidosis?
exp: The 1-2-3 sign (Garland triad) refers to bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy plus right paratracheal lymphadenopathy on a frontal chest X-ray, and is a classic, though not specific, finding in stage I pulmonary sarcoidosis.

subject: Radiology
q: Image described: Plain X-ray KUB showing a large radio-opaque calculus filling the renal pelvis and extending into multiple calyces in a branching, antler-like pattern. What is the most likely composition of this stone?
why: Calcium oxalate stones are radio-opaque but usually small, not staghorn
Correct: staghorn calculi are classically struvite, formed in alkaline urine from urease-producing organisms such as Proteus
Uric acid stones are radiolucent on a plain film
Cystine stones are faintly opaque and less often staghorn
exp: A staghorn calculus filling the pelvicalyceal system is classically struvite. It forms in alkaline urine generated by urease-producing organisms (Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella), is radio-opaque, and usually requires PCNL for complete clearance.

subject: Radiology
q: Image described: lateral skull/OPG radiograph shows an elongated, calcified styloid process (over 2.5 cm) on one side in a 45-year-old with vague throat pain and pain on neck rotation. What is the diagnosis?
why: elongated calcified styloid process over 2.5 cm confirms Eagle syndrome
sialolithiasis shows a radiopaque stone in the submandibular duct, not an elongated styloid
retropharyngeal abscess shows prevertebral soft-tissue widening, not a bony/calcified process
thyroglossal duct cyst is a midline neck cyst on ultrasound, unrelated to styloid calcification
exp: Eagle syndrome results from elongation of the styloid process (over 2.5-3 cm) or calcification of the stylohyoid ligament, causing recurrent throat/neck pain, foreign-body sensation, and pain on head rotation or swallowing due to compression of adjacent cranial nerves (IX, X) and carotid vessels. Diagnosis is confirmed on lateral skull X-ray, OPG, or CT with 3D reconstruction; treatment is styloidectomy for symptomatic cases.

subject: Radiology
q: Image described: contrast CT abdomen shows a well-defined right renal mass with regions of negative Hounsfield units (-20 to -80 HU) consistent with macroscopic fat, no calcification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: RCC does not contain macroscopic fat
oncocytoma shows a central stellate scar, not fat
negative-HU regions equal macroscopic fat, virtually diagnostic of angiomyolipoma
Wilms tumour is a paediatric mixed solid mass without fat, shows the claw sign
exp: Angiomyolipoma is a benign renal tumour composed of blood vessels, smooth muscle, and mature fat; the presence of macroscopic fat (negative HU) on CT is virtually diagnostic and distinguishes it from renal cell carcinoma, which almost never contains fat. Larger angiomyolipomas (over 4 cm) carry a risk of spontaneous haemorrhage and may need embolization.

subject: Radiology
q: Image described: chest X-ray shows an S-shaped contour formed by an elevated horizontal fissure combined with a central hilar mass in a 62-year-old smoker. What does this finding indicate?
opts: Golden S sign of right upper lobe collapse from a central obstructing mass
Scimitar sign of anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
why: elevated fissure plus central mass is the classic Golden S sign of obstructive lobar collapse
Westermark sign is focal oligaemia distal to an occluded pulmonary vessel in PE, not fissure distortion
scimitar sign is a curvilinear vein shadow from anomalous pulmonary venous drainage to the IVC, seen in children
deep sulcus sign is a lucent, deepened costophrenic angle on a supine film in pneumothorax
exp: The Golden S sign occurs when right upper lobe collapse combines with a central hilar or perihilar mass; the collapsed lobe's medial part is pulled up by volume loss while the mass bulges outward, producing an S-shaped fissure on chest X-ray. It is a classic clue to an obstructing central bronchogenic carcinoma and mandates further evaluation with CT and bronchoscopy.

subject: Radiology
q: Which radioactive source is standard for high-dose-rate (HDR) intracavitary brachytherapy in carcinoma cervix?
why: cobalt-60 is chiefly a teletherapy (external beam) source, not the standard HDR brachytherapy source
caesium-137 was used for older low-dose-rate brachytherapy, now largely phased out
iodine-131 is a therapeutic isotope for thyroid disease, unrelated to brachytherapy
iridium-192's high specific activity and compact size make it the standard HDR afterloading source
exp: Iridium-192 is the standard source used in modern high-dose-rate remote afterloading brachytherapy systems for carcinoma cervix and other gynaecological/head-neck cancers, because its small size, high specific activity, and intermediate energy allow rapid treatment with a miniaturized source on a robotic afterloader. Cobalt-60 and caesium-137 have largely been replaced for intracavitary HDR use.
